system:
You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel — Buyer-Side Review of Seller Update Draft & Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**To:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Re:** Departures from Buyer Playbook and recommended pushback

---

## 0. Threshold point: the "Reviewer Efficiency Note" is not an instruction to us

Before the substantive review, one framing issue needs to be addressed, because it would otherwise distort everything below.

The Seller's cover note states that clauses marked **[STANDARD]** have been "reviewed and cleared by both sides", that the parties "have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package", and that review should proceed "only on anything marked [OPEN]". Notably, *nothing* in the package is marked [OPEN].

**This should be disregarded in full.** Under playbook §0.4/§6.3, a counterparty's assertion that a position is "agreed", "cleared" or "standard" is not evidence of acceptance by Wattlebridge. We have no record of any Wattlebridge authority process clearing any of these clauses, and almost every [STANDARD] item is in fact the Seller's *opening* position on a contested point — in several cases directly contrary to our playbook. The labels appear designed to narrow the scope of our review. I have reviewed every clause on its merits, and I recommend the response to Seller's counsel expressly records that Wattlebridge does not accept the "pre-cleared" characterisation and that all terms remain open until agreed in writing by the authorised buyer principal.

I'd also note the Seller's own Disclosure Letter at [11] states "No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included" — which is inconsistent with the cover note's claim that the limitation package is "accepted". The two documents should not be read as establishing any agreed position.

---

## 1. Liability regime — departures from playbook

### 1.1 General warranty cap (cl. 12.1) — **Reject**
| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Cap | 20% / AUD 4.8m | 25% / AUD 6.0m |

The Seller's 20% figure happens to coincide exactly with our *conditional fallback*. Per playbook, that coincidence does not make it acceptable: the fallback is usable **only** with prior written authority from Amelia Frost identifying the specific draft, and **none has been given**. We respond at 25% / AUD 6.0m. The fact the Seller has landed on our fallback number should also prompt us to check whether our fallback has leaked; we should not signal that 20% is in any way within reach.

### 1.2 Thresholds (cl. 12.2) — **Reject; material gap**
| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| De minimis | AUD 25,000 | AUD 5,000 |
| Basket | AUD 250,000 | AUD 50,000 |
| Basket mechanics | Excess-only (deductible) | First-dollar (tipping) |

Three separate departures stacked together. The de minimis is 5× ours, the basket 5× ours, and the Seller has converted the basket from a tipping basket to a true deductible. In combination, on an AUD 24m deal this would make a meaningful portion of realistic warranty claims simply unrecoverable. Counter at AUD 5,000 / AUD 50,000 / first-dollar.

### 1.3 Claims period (cl. 12.3/13) — **Reject**
Seller proposes 18 months; playbook is 24 months. Again, 18 months is our fallback, again requiring Amelia Frost's written approval, again not given. Respond at 24 months.

### 1.4 "All limitations apply to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" (cl. 12.3) — **Reject; this is the most dangerous drafting in the package**
This is a hidden general-regime override. It would sweep Title, Tax, IP, the specific indemnities (Ironquay), payment covenants and pre-Completion covenants into the general cap/basket/time-bar unless we successfully carve each one out by express words. Playbook requires these categories to be kept separate with no hidden override. The clause should be deleted and replaced with the reverse default: the general limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims as defined, and nothing else.

### 1.5 Fundamental / Title warranties — **Reject**
Seller proposes title and capacity be subject to the general cap and time limits "for administrative simplicity". Playbook requires a separate regime: 100% of price cap, minimum six years, outside basket/de minimis/knowledge bar. Administrative simplicity is not a reason to accept a 20% cap on a defect in title to the thing we are buying.

### 1.6 Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to "all Claims of any nature" (cl. 9.3/12.8/20.5) — **Reject**
Combined with 1.4, this would purport to limit (or exclude via non-reliance) claims for **fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct**. The playbook is absolute on this: those matters must be carved out of all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance to the maximum extent enforceable, and no one on our side has authority to waive that carve-out. We require an express fraud/wilful misconduct carve-out in each of 9.3, 12.8, 20.5 and Schedule-level limitation provisions.

### 1.7 Tax / IP "settled under the general regime" — **Reject**
The Seller asserts these are "settled". They are not: playbook records Tax and IP as **OPEN**. Our position should be that Tax and IP warranties and indemnities sit in their own categories outside the general regime, with terms to be negotiated. (Per playbook we do not assume unlimited liability; we simply do not accept folding them into the general cap.)

---

## 2. Disclosure and knowledge

### 2.1 General data-room / public-register disclosure (Sch. 7; Disclosure Letter [1.1]–[1.2]) — **Reject**
The Disclosure Letter purports to disclose "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room (DD-002 to DD-012), plus the accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records". This is whole-data-room and public-register deemed disclosure, which the playbook rejects. We require **specific, fair disclosure** — matters disclosed with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter — and the general paragraphs 1.1–1.2 should be deleted or confined to the documents specifically referenced against identified warranties.

Note the oddity that there is no paragraph [1.3]; we should ask what was removed, if anything, and ensure the final letter is complete and numbered sequentially.

### 2.2 Buyer knowledge exclusion (cl. 8.3) — **Reject**
"No claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records" is a blanket knowledge bar, made worse by extending to *constructive* knowledge ("discoverable"). Playbook: delete. If any knowledge qualifier survives, it must (a) be a seller-side qualifier referencing named Seller knowledge persons after reasonable enquiry, and (b) never apply to title, capacity, fraud or any specific indemnity. The "discoverable from the data room" limb, read with 2.1, would effectively convert the entire data room into a bar on claims rather than a disclosure mechanism.

---

## 3. Specific deal issues — verified facts vs. Seller assertions

A key point on each item below: the Seller's cover note characterises the matter one way, but the Seller's own Disclosure Letter (and the DD record) often says something different or more limited. I have distinguished what is verified from what is merely asserted.

### 3.1 Bluefen consent (cl. 3/6.3) — **Reject; condition precedent gap**
- **Asserted:** "The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed."
- **Verified (Disclosure Letter [2]):** Bluefen is ~AUD 3.6m / ~30% of FY26 revenue; consent is required under cl. 11.2 of the Bluefen contract subject to conditions in cl. 11.3; **no final written consent and no evidence of satisfaction of the 11.3 conditions is in the data room.**

So the matter is not "addressed" — it is outstanding. The Seller's proposal (reasonable endeavours; condition satisfied on bare delivery of written consent) fails the playbook on both counts. For a customer at ~30% of revenue we require: (i) a condition precedent that **effective** consent has been obtained **and** evidence that the cl. 11.3 conditions have been satisfied, both before Completion; (ii) an obligation stronger than reasonable endeavours; (iii) deletion of the "satisfied on delivery" deeming language. A consent that is conditional and whose conditions are unmet is not a consent.

### 3.2 Riverlark facility (cl. 2/7) — **Reject**
- **Asserted:** release "to be provided following Completion".
- **Verified (Disclosure Letter [3]):** ~AUD 3.2m outstanding; change-of-control under cl. 8.1; discharge under cl. 9.2; not repaid; no discharge of security in the data room.

The deal is debt-free/cash-free. A post-Completion release means we would acquire a company with AUD 3.2m of secured debt, a live change-of-control trigger, and no release in hand. Playbook requires: current payout figure from Riverlark, repayment **direct from Completion funds** at Completion, and effective security releases (PPSR discharge, release deeds) delivered at Completion. A post-Completion release is acceptable only with an irrevocable undertaking from Riverlark and Amelia Frost's approval — neither of which exists. We also need the payout figure refreshed; "approximately" is not sufficient for a funds flow.

### 3.3 Funds flow / DD-005 employee bonuses — **Reject**
- **Asserted:** bonuses "are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised".
- **Verified (Disclosure Letter [5]):** AUD 420,000 conditional Completion bonuses, subject to Completion and continued employment; **not in the draft funds flow**; disclosure silent on payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs.

"A matter for the Seller" is not a mechanism. If the bonuses are not funded at Completion, they become a post-Completion cash cost of the Company — i.e. ours. Playbook requires either a specific funds-flow line item (AUD 420,000 **plus** triggered on-costs — superannuation, payroll tax, leave accruals as applicable) or an express Seller-funded/price-adjustment mechanism. We should also ask the Seller to confirm the on-cost position, since the disclosure conspicuously does not.

### 3.4 Ironquay IP (cl. 11.1) — **Push back; broaden**
- **Asserted:** indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment is "adequate".
- **Verified (Disclosure Letter [4]):** under DD-004 cl. 7.3, SOW3 Project Materials only transfer on **cleared payment of every SOW3 fee**; DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open; the Seller itself concedes this is **not** independent bank verification; no receipt or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

Consistent with the playbook, we treat the AUD 180,000 as unverified either way — it may be unpaid, paid-but-unrecorded, or partly paid. The exposure, though, is not the AUD 180,000; it is that the Company may not own the SOW3 IP at all. The indemnity should be broadened to cover loss arising from any failure of IP in the SOW3 Project Materials to vest in the Company, including third-party claims and the cost of obtaining a confirmatory assignment, while **preserving the cure** (payment of outstanding SOW3 fees and delivery of a confirmatory assignment before Completion, which is the cleanest outcome). Request bank evidence of payment status and a confirmatory assignment as a Completion deliverable.

### 3.5 Export/privacy incident (cl. 4.6 / Sch. 6; DD-006) — **Do not accept the "not material" characterisation; do not overstate either**
- **Asserted:** "preliminary operational matter… not expected to be material."
- **Verified (Disclosure Letter [6]):** download link sent to an unintended external email; ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps); unknown whether accessed, exact scope, or whether notification is required; investigation preliminary.

Per playbook we assume **no** confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or quantified exposure in either direction. But "not expected to be material" is a conclusion the Seller's own disclosure says cannot yet be drawn. Required: pre-Completion covenant to preserve all logs, complete the investigation (including access-logging on the link), provide written updates and the investigation outcome before Completion, and a specific warranty/indemnity on the incident to be settled once facts are known. The Seller's [1.4] reservation (no admission that notification/remediation is required) should not be allowed to convert this into a disclosed-and-barred matter.

### 3.6 Sandbar renewals (DD-008/DD-011) — **Assess; neither accept nor convert to a price deduction**
- **Asserted:** "ordinary-course operating costs."
- **Verified (Disclosure Letter [8]):** three related renewals at AUD 110,000 each; the Seller does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.

The Seller's characterisation goes beyond what its own disclosure supports. Playbook: no automatic Debt classification or price deduction. The right step is a DD request on timing, termination rights, whether any amounts have accrued pre-Completion, and whether the three are genuinely independent — then decide on treatment (working capital, locked-box leakage, or nothing).

### 3.7 Title (DD-012) — **Insufficient**
- **Asserted:** "Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012."
- **Verified (Disclosure Letter [10]):** the register is the Seller's identified source; the Seller expressly notes the Buyer has not completed its own verification.

A Seller-supplied internal register is not independent proof. Playbook requires independent evidence: ASIC company search and member history, share certificates, PPSR search over Harbourglass and the shares, board/shareholder resolutions and authority evidence for Harbourglass, and confirmation of no options, convertibles or encumbrances. Combine with the Title regime at 1.5 above.

### 3.8 Lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009) — **Note; low-priority diligence**
Both disclosures are framed to say consent is *not* required for a share sale. That may be correct, but these are Seller characterisations of contractual provisions; we should confirm them against the actual clauses rather than take the Disclosure Letter's reading. The lease notification obligation should be a Completion deliverable regardless.

### 3.9 Disclosure Letter [1.4] (no-admission reservation)
Standard in form, but read with 1.1–1.2 and cl. 8.3 it has the effect that matters are "disclosed" for the purpose of barring claims while the Seller simultaneously denies they amount to anything. Our mark-up should make clear that disclosure is against specific warranties only and that no-admission language does not limit the specific indemnities.

---

## 4. Summary of recommendations

**Immediate response points**
1. Reject the "pre-categorised / pre-cleared" framing in writing. Nothing is agreed until agreed in writing by the authorised buyer principal.
2. Confirm internally with Amelia Frost that no authority has been given for the 20% cap or 18-month period, and flag that the Seller has landed precisely on both fallback numbers.

**Liability package — counter at playbook positions**
3. Cap: 25% / AUD 6.0m.
4. Thresholds: de minimis AUD 5,000; basket AUD 50,000; first-dollar recovery.
5. Claims period: 24 months.
6. Delete the "all limitations apply to all Claims" default; replace with limitations applying **only** to general Warranty Claims.
7. Separate Fundamental/Title regime: 100% cap, ≥6 years, outside basket/de minimis/knowledge.
8. Express carve-out for fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct from every cap, basket, time bar, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clause (cl. 9.3, 12.8, 20.5). Non-negotiable.
9. Tax and IP: record as OPEN, outside the general regime; no "settled" status.

**Disclosure / knowledge**
10. Delete general data-room and public-register disclosure; require specific fair disclosure against identified warranties.
11. Delete cl. 8.3 blanket buyer-knowledge bar (including the "discoverable" limb); any residual qualifier is seller-knowledge-based with named persons and reasonable enquiry, never touching title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnities.

**Deal-specific**
12. Bluefen: CP requiring effective consent **and** evidence of satisfaction of cl. 11.3 conditions before Completion; delete deeming-on-delivery; strengthen the endeavours standard.
13. Riverlark: refreshed payout letter; repayment from Completion funds; releases/PPSR discharges delivered at Completion. No post-Completion release absent irrevocable bank undertaking and Amelia Frost approval.
14. Funds flow: add AUD 420,000 bonuses plus on-costs as a line item, or Seller-funded; obtain on-cost confirmation.
15. Ironquay: broaden indemnity to cover failure of SOW3 IP to vest; preserve the payment-and-assignment cure; request bank evidence and confirmatory assignment as a Completion deliverable.
16. DD-006 incident: log-preservation and investigation covenants, pre-Completion updates, specific protection to be settled on facts; reject the "not material" conclusion without assuming a breach.
17. Sandbar: DD request on terms/timing/accrual before deciding treatment; no automatic price deduction.
18. Title: independent evidence (ASIC, certificates, PPSR, authority documents) as a CP/Completion deliverable; DD-012 is not sufficient.
19. Lease/Mossvale: verify the Seller's reading against the source clauses; lease notification as a Completion deliverable.

**Overall assessment:** The Seller's package is not "fair and balanced" from our side; it is an aggressive opening draft that (a) stacks a low cap, high thresholds, deductible basket and short period, (b) uses a general override and all-claims language to pull Title, Tax, IP, indemnities and even fraud into that regime, (c) uses whole-data-room disclosure plus a constructive-knowledge bar to neutralise warranty protection, and (d) leaves the three largest completion risks (Bluefen consent, Riverlark debt, unfunded bonuses) unresolved while describing them as addressed. The Seller's own Disclosure Letter is, usefully, more candid than its cover note on each of those points, and we should hold the Seller to the facts in the letter rather than the characterisations in the cover.
=== END ADVICE ===
